analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to have brake-override technology, event data recorders, and public defect disclosure, and sharply raises penalties on automakers that hide safety defects.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate calendar in November 2010, but the full Senate never voted before the Congress ended — leaving the safety standards, the $300 million penalty ceiling, and the whistleblower protections unenacted.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill responded to concerns about sudden, unintended acceleration in cars. It would have required automakers to install brake-override technology and other safety equipment in new cars, put data recorders in every new vehicle, publish the defect reports they send to regulators, raise fines for hiding safety defects from $15 million to up to $300 million, and protect auto industry employees who report safety problems. It passed out of the Senate Commerce Committee but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drives or rides in a car. The bill would require new cars to stop even when the accelerator is stuck (brake override), set pedal-clearance and electronics-performance standards, standardize push-button ignition and gear-shifter controls, and put event data recorders in all new passenger cars by model year 2015 and heavy trucks by 2017 — with the recorder's data owned by the vehicle owner and protected against retrieval without the owner's consent, a court order, or a safety-agency use that does not reveal who the driver is [S3][S4]. It would raise penalties on automakers that hide defects, let regulators order an immediate halt to sales of a vehicle posing an imminent hazard, make manufacturers' defect reports (Early Warning data) public, create whistleblower protections for auto industry employees, require a written disclosure of unremedied defects to used-car buyers, require quiet electric and hybrid vehicles to make an alert sound for blind pedestrians, and fund research on technology to prevent drunk driving [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every new car would have to stop under normal braking even when the accelerator is at full throttle, with redundant circuits to keep control if a throttle circuit fails, and the Secretary would set standards for pedal clearance, vehicle electronics, push-button ignition emergency shutoff, and gear-shifter labeling.

Event data recorders would become mandatory in all new passenger cars in model year 2015 and in medium- and heavy-duty vehicles by 2017, with the recorded data owned by the vehicle's owner and retrievable only with the owner's consent, a court order, emergency medical need, or a safety-agency investigation that does not disclose who the owner or driver is.

Maximum civil penalties for safety violations would rise from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation and from $15 million to $300 million for a related series, and regulators would gain power to order an immediate stop to production and sale of a vehicle presenting an imminent hazard of death or serious injury.

Manufacturers' defect reports to regulators — Early Warning data — would be disclosed to the public with a presumption in favor of maximum availability, and recall information would have to be searchable online by make, model, and VIN.

Employees of manufacturers, parts suppliers, and dealerships could not be fired or penalized for reporting motor vehicle defects or safety violations, with reinstatement, back pay, and compensatory damages available.

Chief executives would have to personally certify information submitted in NHTSA safety investigations, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per day and added criminal prison time for knowingly submitting misleading information about defects.

Former NHTSA employees with safety responsibilities could not work for or represent automakers for 36 months, with penalties on the automaker of at least $100,000 plus 90% of the employee's compensation.

Used-car dealers would have to tell buyers in writing about any unremedied safety defects, quiet electric and hybrid vehicles would need an alert sound so blind pedestrians can hear them, and research on in-vehicle alcohol detection technology would be funded.

analysis.who_pays: Motor vehicle manufacturers bear the main cost: new federal standards for braking, pedals, electronics, and ignition systems, civil penalties raised from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation and from $15 million to $300 million per related series of violations, a new power for regulators to order an immediate stop-sale on dangerous vehicles, public disclosure of internal defect data, CEO certification of submissions to regulators with civil and criminal penalties for false statements, and a 36-month ban on hiring recent NHTSA employees. Dealers would have to disclose unremedied defects in writing to used-car buyers, and parts suppliers and dealerships would face liability for retaliating against whistleblowing employees [S3][S4]. Some compliance costs would likely be passed into new-vehicle prices [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Car manufacturers, dealers, and parts suppliers

drawbacks.text: New mandatory equipment — brake-override systems, tamper-resistant event data recorders, and revised electronics — would add cost to every new vehicle, and the bill gives manufacturers up to two model years of lead time to comply, a timeline that implies the costs would show up in new-car prices.
The bill itself acknowledges the penalty increases could fall unevenly, requiring the Secretary to weigh the 'potential for undue adverse economic impacts on small business' when setting penalties.

Mandating event data recorders in every new car expands the amount of driving data collected; the bill manages this by making the data the owner's property and barring retrieval without the owner's consent, a court order, or safety-agency use that does not identify the driver, but privacy tradeoffs remain.

Several standards, including pedal placement and gear-shifter labeling, are 'consider' provisions that only require a rulemaking or an explanation of why no standard is warranted, so the bill's real bite depends heavily on later regulatory decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits are broad and concrete: every new car would have been required to stop even with a stuck accelerator, safety defects would have been harder to hide, penalties for concealment would have been 20 times higher, and the employees best positioned to spot defects would have had legal protection for speaking up. The costs are real but narrower — compliance expenses built into new-car prices and some regulatory burden on manufacturers — and the bill itself built in lead time and small-business considerations to soften them. The main complaint about the outcome is not the design but the fate: a bill that cleared its committee with room to spare was never allowed a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee passed it and put it on the calendar, but the full Senate never got around to voting on it before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 4, 2010, with nine cosponsors, and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The committee held a hearing on May 19, 2010, and on June 9, 2010 voted to report the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On November 29, 2010 the committee reported the bill to the Senate and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 653.
The committee's written report was filed on December 21, 2010, but the Senate never took a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Car manufacturers and dealers are better off: none of the new braking, electronics, and recorder requirements, the $300 million penalty ceiling, the public defect-data disclosure, the whistleblower protections, or the 36-month revolving-door ban on hiring former NHTSA staff ever took effect through this bill.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-WV), Chairman, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, chaired the Senate Commerce Committee, held a hearing, reported it favorably with an amendment, placed it on the Senate calendar, and filed the committee's written report.

against.name: Auto manufacturers
against.role: Automaker trade associations and major vehicle manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the sweeping new safety mandates, sharply higher penalties, public disclosure of defect data, and the anti-revolving-door provision during the 2010 debate over the House and Senate safety bills.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011, despite its placement on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred; sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided, with 8 of 56 Senate Democrats and 1 of 42 Senate Republicans cosponsoring.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed new braking, pedal, electronics, and ignition standards on every new vehicle, raised maximum civil penalties for safety violations from $15 million to $300 million per related series, let regulators order immediate stop-sales of dangerous vehicles, made the industry's defect reports public, held chief executives personally liable for false statements to regulators, and banned hiring former NHTSA safety officials for 36 months. Automakers opposed the bill and it never reached a floor vote.

Whistleblower protections would have covered dealership employees, and dealers would have had to give used-car buyers written notice of any unremedied safety defects and obtain written acknowledgment.
Part suppliers would have been liable for retaliating against employees who report defects, and the NHTSA hotline would let their personnel report potential defects directly and confidentially.
